chunks.text: nine out of ten people hate this developer. The one that doesn't automate anything. And if you're watching this, the likelihood is that you're that developer. So how can you automate your deployments so that you never have to deal with another deployment error ever again? CI/CD, or continuous integration and continuous delivery is the practice

of automating the manual tasks that us mere mortals usually have to do when we're deploying our code to production. Things like compiling our code, or running tests or uploading our code to our cloud infrastructure. Automating things not only helps to save a lot of time, it also removes the possibility of human error causing your entire system

to burn to the ground. There are a bunch of tools out there that can help you get started with CI/CD, and I've used a few of them. All of them are great at what they do. However, in this video we're going to be focusing specifically on GitHub Actions. Let's get started. Ultimately, all you need to get started is a GitHub Repository.

If you don't have one, I'm going to leave a link in the description below to the one I'm using for this video. At the top of your repository page, you should see the “Actions” tab. Once you have some automations running on your repository, this is where you can keep track of the logs for each workflow every time they are run. When it's running,

we can see the progress of each step in the GitHub Actions workflow. So if the workflow fails during some tests we know that the code is broken and therefore we don't want to deploy it to our server. If the workflow is successful, we're going to see a big green checkmark telling us that everything is working within our code base.

One of the great things that developers really like about GitHub Actions is that it comes with a bunch of different templates that you can use to easily run specific actions. However, for this video, we're going to create our own from scratch. To do this, you can create a new Yaml file inside of the GitHub workflows directory of your project.

We're going to give our workflow a name and create our trigger, which is going to tell GitHub Actions when we want to run our workflow. You can run workflows using a variety of triggers. For example, every time we push code to our main branch, we might want to deploy it

to our production server automatically so that we don't have to do it ourselves. Or every time we create a new pull request, we might want to test the code to make sure that everything is working before we merge that code into our main branch. These are actually the two examples that we're going to build today.

There's a huge list of different triggers that you can use within GitHub Actions. So if you want to find out more about them, I'd recommend visiting this page on the GitHub documentation. Anyway, because this workflow is going to be used to test our code, we're going to run it every time a pull request to the main branch is created.

So let's say I've got this really cool feature that I want to merge into my main branch. I'd create a pull request which would trigger this workflow. Next, we can create a list of jobs that we want to include in our workflow. We're going to call our job “test” and then we're going to define the operating system that we want the job to run on.

There are other options that you can use. But realistically, Ubuntu is the most common one that people will use within GitHub Actions. And we're going to use a Node.js container because in this example we're using Node.js for our project. That will automatically install Node.js for us

so that we don't have to do it manually through the command line using Ubuntu. It just saves a bit of time. The first step is going to be adding our code to our virtual environments using the checkout action. Now I want you to have a think about the steps that you would take if you were testing your code manually.

Firstly, you’d want to make sure that all of your dependencies have been installed for your project. We can do this by running “npm ci” which is going to run a clean install. Once your dependencies have been installed, you can run your tests using whatever library you're using in your project.

I tend to use Jest when I'm working with a JavaScript project. And then finally I'm going to run the build script, which is going to compile our project. We can commit this code to our repository. And then I'm going to create an example pull request for this really cool feature that I've just built. As you can see, the GitHub Actions

workflow is going to spin up a virtual environment, run our tests and then confirm that our code is working as expected. So automatically, I know the code is working without having to pull the pull request onto my local machine and then running the test manually. Now that we know that our code is going to be working,

when we merge it into the main branch, we want to figure out how we can use GitHub Actions to automatically deploy our code to our production infrastructure. This is the continuous delivery or CD part of the process. If we weren't automating anything, your deployment process may look a little like this. First I'm going to run “git pull”

to get the latest version of my code from our repository. Then I'm going to run “git checkout” to make sure that I'm in my main branch. Run “npm install”, “npm run build”, and then deploy my code to the server using this long command, which I might get wrong. Oh, and then ssh into the server to install the dependencies

and restart the Node.js process. Okay, as you can see, this took a long time and it was pretty complicated for such a small project. So let's automate this. We're going to create another Yaml file inside of our GitHub workflows directory, which is going to be triggered every time some code gets pushed to our main branch.

Inside of this workflow, we're going to run a job which is going to build our project and then deploy it to our server. Like we did with our testing workflow, we're going to run our job on Ubuntu, checkout the code and install Node.js. We're going to run “npm ci” to do a clean install of the project's dependencies, and then run the build script.

Once the build is completed, we're going to deploy our code using SCP, which is going to upload all of our files to the server. Because access to our server is protected using SSH keys, we need to take an SSH key that has access to our server and add the content of it to our GitHub Actions secrets. This is where you can store sensitive credentials

that need to be used within your GitHub Actions, but can't be stored within your repository for security reasons. For example your Stripe or OpenAI keys. You wouldn't want to put them in your repository. I've also added the address of the server that we're going to be deploying our code to, as well as the username that I have on the server.

We can then access our secrets within our GitHub Actions workflow and add our SSH key to our virtual environment. Now we can upload our files to our server using SCP in the exact same way that we would have done it using the command line. The final step in our deployment process is to SSH enter the server,

install the dependencies, and then restart the Node.js process. In this case I'm using PM2 to manage the Node.js process. You can test your workflow using Act which allows you to run GitHub Action scripts offline. To do this, you need to have Docker running on your local machine as well as create a “.secrets” file within your project directory.

That secrets file is then going to be used to replace what would be GitHub Actions secrets. So make sure you don't actually put your deployment secrets in that file. You need to put some test ones in that you're maybe deploying to different infrastructure. Because you wouldn't want to run a test on actual production infrastructure.

You can then run the “act” command to test your workflow and make sure that everything is working correctly. Once you're happy with your workflow, you can publish it to your GitHub repository. Now, if we merge that super cool feature that we were testing earlier, you can see that we've triggered this automated workflow

which is going to deploy our code to our production server. So now you can say that you understand CI/CD. If you learned something in today's video, please do leave a like down below and subscribe for more coding videos.
